Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for Australia's chase! Dew, or no dew, is the question. And how will that affect the bowling? We shall find that out sooner. Now then, the Proteas spread out of the huddle and take their spots on the field. Mitchell Marsh and Travis Head will open for 'Straya'. Nandre Burger has the new ball and is raring to go. Let's play...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right. 297 is the magic number for Australia to maintain an unbeaten record at Cazaly's Stadium. But in chasing a total as challenging as this, or in any run chase for that matter, a good start with the bat is a non-negotiable, as chasing hasn't been THAT easy here. South Africa will be without the services of their premier pacer Kagiso Rabada and it will be interesting to see how they restrict this Australian side laden with power hitters. Spin has been effective and the likes of Keshav Maharaj and Prenelan Subrayen could prove to be crucial. Stick around, as the run chase is on the other side very shortly.

Australia's Travis Head is up for a quick chat. He says that bowling 8-9 overs wasn't on the bingo for him, but after 4-5 overs, it felt good to bowl. Adds that he tried to get out of the hitting range of Dewald Brevis but he still tried to take him on and they've seen how destructive he can be in the T20s. Mentions that he and Mitch will look to maximize the Powerplay, especially with the wind playing a part but there might be some dew as we saw in the last T20I.

But despite that collapse, South Africa managed to score 73 runs in the last 10 overs on the back of pivotal lower order contributions. We all know that Wiaan Mulder can prove to be quite handy with the bat and he ensured that he stays till the end. His cameo of 31 off just 26 balls propelled the Saffas to 296. From an Australian bowling perspective, they used as many as seven bowlers, but the spinners proved to be more effective with Adam Zampa and Travis Head sharing 5 wickets between them. However, it was surprising to see Josh Hazlewood not bowling his full quota of ten overs, given how disciplined he was.

Australia tightened their lines and lengths in the middle overs, forcing the batters to take risks to keep the scoreboard moving. But wickets didn’t fall in clusters. South Africa kept building partnerships, with Breetzke and Bavuma steering the innings steadily. With the pitch offering grip and the spinners in control, Labuschagne was brought in as a third spin option to add more variety and keep the pressure on. But it was Travis Head who fished out to the big hitters, claiming a four-for. The big highlight of his bowling was him fishing out Tristan Stubbs and Dewald Brevis, just when the Proteas were about to motor in the final ten overs. With those quick fall of wickets, South Africa slipped from a comfortable 223/2 to 230/5.

As soon as the fielding restrictions were lifted, Marsh turned to spin. Zampa and Head bowled in tandem and started getting noticeable turn. The openers looked a bit hesitant, and a few false strokes crept in as the ball began to grip. Head eventually broke the 92-run stand. Even though the spinners were tricky, the pacers became easier to handle, especially as the ball softened up, making strokeplay more comfortable. Markram kept the tempo up, but once he departed for 82, the innings slowed and boundaries became harder to find.

With hardly any grass on the pitch, it looked like a decent surface for batting. But early on, Hazlewood and Dwarshuis found just enough movement and nip off the deck to keep the openers quiet. They bowled tight lines, making sure the batters couldn’t swing freely. But once that early movement faded, Markram and Rickelton began to settle in. They weren't flashy, but showed good composure while being watchful. They saw off the first line of Australia's bowling attack safely and posted 56 runs in the first Powerplay without losing a wicket.

Not quite sure which side will be more pleased with this score on the board. Australia might feel a bit good to restrict South Africa below 300, but given the circumstances South Africa were in before the start of the final Powerplay, they have recovered pretty well with the lower order chipping in with handy contributions. This is also the highest first-inning ODI total in Cairns, and with 11 runs coming off the last over, the Proteas would have a slight momentum going back into the sheds. But through and through, as has been the case in this white-ball series so far, both teams have traded blows equally and momentum hasn't stayed with one side for long.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. Australia have shown good discipline with the ball as spin has been effective, and a few chances here and there have been created. However, the Aussies haven't been able to string wickets in clusters, which has allowed the Proteas to string partnerships. With 8 wickets in hand and a couple of proper hitters yet to come, the tourists seem to be off to a big total on a slow pitch. Currently, this stand between Matthew Breetzke and skipper Temba Bavuma has stitched together 53 runs, and Australia are in search of a breakthrough. A couple of quick wickets moving towards the climax of the innings could prove handy. But they need them now. A change in bowling as Aaron Hardie returns for another spell. He is 1-0-13-0 so far. Also, as per the new ICC rules, it seems like Australia have picked one ball of the two to continue till the end of the innings.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. Mitchell Marsh has smartly brought spin in tandem and the ball has gripped evidently. Ryan Rickelton, in particular, looked tentative against the two spinners before perishing. Commentary.Commentary: All in readiness for the game to begin! The umpires are out in the middle and so are the players of Australia. It will be the same opening pairing as the T20Is for South Africa, with Aiden Markram and Ryan Rickelton striding out to the middle. Josh Hazlewood will take the first new ball and he is raring to go. Let's play...

It is time to listen to Australia's Marnus Labuschagne who came for a quick chat. Marnus says that it's been good after coming back from the West Indies and has had time to work on his game. Reckons that form isn't necessarily the same across all formats, and he tries to separate the red-ball and the white-ball format. Adds that he's mostly batted at number 4 and 5 in ODIs, so batting at number 3 is an opportunity, and hopefully, he can do well.
Australia (Playing XI) - Mitchell Marsh (C), Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis (WK), Alex Carey, Aaron Hardie, Ben Dwarshuis, Nathan Ellis, Adam Zampa and Josh Hazlewood.

South Africa (Playing XI) - Aiden Markram, Ryan Rickelton (WK), Temba Bavuma (C), Matthew Breetzke, Tristan Stubbs, Dewald Brevis (On ODI debut), Wiaan Mulder, Keshav Maharaj, Prenelan Subrayen (On ODI debut), Nandre Burger and Lungi Ngidi.

The captain of South Africa, Temba Bavuma, says that they would have bowled first as well, as this is what the stat says. Informs that Dewald Brevis is surely playing and Prenelan Subrayen also makes it to the side, and he is excited to see what these guys can do in the longer format. He further stresses on adapting the conditions well. Also mentions that if the conditions demands them to play in a certain way, they would like to do so.

The Australian skipper, Mitchell Marsh, says that the wicket looks dry, but the dew should set in as well. Adds that they are a really well-connected group, who play for Australia and like to win. Informs that there are no surprises as the likes of Marnus Labuschagne and Alex Carey come into the team.
TOSS UPDATE - The flip of the coin is won by Mitchell Marsh and he elects what he loves to do the most. Australia have elected to BOWL first.

UPDATE - We are hearing that South Africa's premier bowler, Kagiso Rabada, has been RULED OUT of the ODI series due to inflammation of his right ankle. According to Cricket South Africa's official post on social media, Rabada underwent a scan on Monday, which revealed the extent of his injury. He will remain in rehab in Australia, and will be monitored by the South African medical staff. This is a huge blow for the Proteas, and it remains to be seen who will make it in the eleven in his absence. They do have a couple of options in their squad - Nandre Burger and Kwena Maphaka - in the pace department.

The last these two sides met in this format was in the 2023 World Cup semifinal, with their previous bilateral series coming just before that mega event. Recent history, though, has gone South Africa’s way as they have won four of the last five series, while Australia’s last series success came way back in 2014/15. Cairns, however, has been a fortress for the hosts with five ODIs played here and not a single defeat. Three matches, two quality sides, and plenty on the line, to stitch a strong future. It is all set up for a cracking series. Will the bowlers rule? Or is it going to be a batter's safe haven? Toss and team news shortly. Stay tuned.

Apart from skipper Temba Bavuma and Aiden Markram holding the batting core, and Kagiso Rabada with Lungi Ngidi leading the bowling, this Proteas lineup is buzzing with youth. Fresh faces, raw energy and a couple of debutants will be stepping straight into the spotlight. It’s a big test, but also a chance to grab this opportunity to make their mark. Alongside them are a few familiar names who’ve forced their way after strong stints in the T20I series across both departments. One such name is Kwena Maphaka, who had a dream run in the T20I series, where he picked up 9 wickets, the most in the series.

Australia still carry plenty of firepower despite a few injury concerns. Travis Head hasn't been in the same form he was back in 2023, Marnus Labuschagne is out to nail down his own spot in the side, and skipper Mitchell Marsh is the man in form up top. The big question, though, is, who after Maxwell? That’s where the likes of Cooper Connolly and Aaron Hardie get thrown into the furnace. The batting may be finding its next gear, but the bowling ranks remain lethal with Josh Hazlewood leading the charge alongside Nathan Ellis and Adam Zampa, alongside some young guns as well.

Australia roll into this series minus a few of their marquee names. Steve Smith and Glenn Maxwell have already stepped away from ODIs, while Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc are sitting this one out to recharge ahead of the Ashes. The Proteas aren’t at full strength either. Marco Jansen remains sidelined with a thumb injury, David Miller is featuring in The Hundred, and Heinrich Klaasen’s retirement leaves a gap in the middle order. And no one carries more hype than Dewald Brevis, who is highly likely to make his ODI debut. After lighting up the T20Is, the stage is wide open for him to stamp himself as South Africa’s next big white-ball hitter.

G’day from Cairns. The T20I leg gave us no dull moment with both sides flexing their depth and skill in equal measure. That chapter is done with the hosts claiming the series that went down to the wire, and the attention now turns to the ODI format. Cazaly’s Stadium takes centre stage for the opener, hosting its first game between Australia and South Africa, before the teams head down to Mackay to wrap up the series. The Aussies return to the format after the Champions Trophy earlier in the year, while South Africa arrive from a tri-series in Zimbabwe, where they stumbled at the final hurdle. With the 2027 ODI World Cup somewhere around the halfway mark, both sides will have an eye on shaping their core, ironing out combinations, and setting down markers for the road ahead. On that note, we welcome you all to our coverage.

The ODI leg of Australia’s home summer kicks off with a mouth-watering clash at the Cazaly's Stadium in Cairns as they take on South Africa in the first of three matches. Australia come in on the back of a 2-1 T20I series win, but they know the Proteas have been their bogey side in recent years, having lost the last four bilateral ODI series between the two, including the last time they met in Australia. Both teams also return to the format after their Champions Trophy heartbreaks, with the hosts falling to India and South Africa being undone by New Zealand in the semifinals. Australia’s strength, as always, lies in their top order with Travis Head and Mitchell Marsh setting the tone, and in-form Cameron Green adding stability in the middle alongside Alex Carey. Josh Inglis’ power-hitting gives them flexibility, but they will only have Josh Hazlewood from the potent pace trio for this series. Supporting him will be Xavier Bartlett and Ben Dwarshuis, with Adam Zampa leading the spin attack. A few of the big names have been rested, which gives the chance to the fringe players to step up and make a mark. South Africa arrive with momentum despite losing the T20Is, thanks largely to the stunning form of Dewald Brevis, who lit up the series with a blistering hundred and a quickfire fifty. He is expected to make his ODI debut and will hopefully continue his good run. Add in the experience of skipper Temba Bavuma and Aiden Markram, and their batting suddenly looks dangerous. The likes of Matthew Breetzke, Tristan Stubbs, and Ryan Rickelton add further depth. Their bowling attack, spearheaded by Kagiso Rabada along with Nandre Burger and Lungi Ngidi, remains top-class in world cricket, with Keshav Maharaj providing control in the middle overs. The concern for them will be finishing games under pressure, something that has haunted South African sides in the past. With history favouring the Proteas and the Aussies eager to reassert dominance at home, this opener promises fireworks. South Africa’s recent edge in ODIs will give them confidence, but with the backing of the home fans, the Aussies will be ready for anything. It’s a clash of pride, power, and pedigree!
